notice: RN bank batch 2: Management of care: prioritization, delegation and communication. Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: The nurse on a surgical unit receives handoff report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 68-year-old with COPD whose SpO2 is 88% on 2 L/min, respirations 24/min, who says the morning breathlessness is usual
A 46-year-old 6 hours after a thyroidectomy who reports tingling around the lips; the voice has been hoarse since surgery
A 72-year-old 2 days after a hip arthroplasty who is suddenly restless, respirations 28/min, SpO2 90% on room air
A 31-year-old with type 1 diabetes whose glucose before breakfast is 288 mg/dL with negative urine ketones

rationale.correct: See first the client with a sudden, unexpected change in breathing or circulation. Expected or baseline abnormal findings (COPD saturations, hoarseness after neck surgery) can wait.

perOption.a: An SpO2 of 88% to 92% is the usual target in COPD, and the client describes a baseline pattern, so this can wait for the first round.
perOption.b: Perioral tingling is an early sign of hypocalcemia and needs a calcium level and assessment soon, but the airway is not yet compromised and hoarseness is expected.
perOption.c: Sudden restlessness, tachypnea and new hypoxemia after hip surgery suggest pulmonary embolism, a life-threatening change from baseline.
perOption.d: Hyperglycemia without ketones needs correction-scale insulin but is not immediately life-threatening.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize a sudden respiratory change over expected abnormal findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients on a medical unit. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client in sickle cell crisis rating pain 9 out of 10, whose last IV morphine was 2 hours ago; the next dose is due in 1 hour
A client with pyelonephritis, temperature 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), heart rate 96/min, blood pressure 122/74, on IV ceftriaxone since this morning
A client admitted with suspected appendicitis who says the pain suddenly got much better; heart rate is now 118/min
A client with gastroenteritis who vomited three times overnight; blood pressure 108/68 lying and 102/64 sitting

rationale.correct: An unexpected improvement in pain with new tachycardia is a red flag. An expected finding, even a severe one, ranks below a sign of a new complication.

perOption.a: Severe pain in sickle cell crisis is expected and treated on a schedule; the nurse can call for an earlier dose after the unstable client is seen.
perOption.b: Fever with mild tachycardia is expected while antibiotics take effect; the blood pressure is stable.
perOption.c: Sudden relief of appendicitis pain followed by new tachycardia suggests perforation, which leads to peritonitis and sepsis.
perOption.d: A small postural drop needs fluids and monitoring but is not yet unstable.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize perforation of the appendix as an emergency.

questions.stem: The charge nurse receives four updates from the nursing team. Which client needs the charge nurse's attention first?

options.text: A client 2 hours after a femoral-approach cardiac catheterization who reports new low back pain; heart rate 112/min
A client with a head injury whose Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14 because of confusion about the date, unchanged since admission
A client with a chest tube for a pneumothorax whose water seal chamber bubbles briefly each time the client coughs
A client receiving IV vancomycin whose trough level has not been drawn and the next dose is due in 60 minutes

rationale.correct: After a femoral puncture, back or flank pain with tachycardia is retroperitoneal bleeding until proven otherwise. Expected and stable findings come later.

perOption.a: New back or flank pain with tachycardia after a femoral puncture suggests retroperitoneal bleeding, which can cause shock with no visible hematoma.
perOption.b: A stable score that matches the admission baseline is reassuring; a drop of 2 or more points would be urgent.
perOption.c: Intermittent bubbling with coughing is expected while air leaves the pleural space; continuous bubbling would suggest a leak.
perOption.d: The trough is drawn within 30 minutes before the dose, so there is still time to obtain it.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize retroperitoneal bleeding after cardiac catheterization.

questions.stem: A client 1 day after an open abdominal surgery rates incisional pain 6 out of 10, is anxious about going home, has a weak cough with coarse crackles in both lower lobes, has had a urine output of 35 mL/hr, and has not yet walked. Which nursing problem is the priority?

options.text: Acute pain related to the abdominal incision
Risk for deficient fluid volume
Ineffective airway clearance
Anxiety related to discharge

rationale.correct: Use airway, breathing, circulation, then Maslow: an actual airway problem comes before pain, risk problems and psychosocial needs. Treating pain can be part of the airway plan.

perOption.a: Pain does need treatment, partly because it stops the client coughing, but it is not the direct threat.
perOption.b: An output of 35 mL/hr is above the 30 mL/hr minimum, and a risk problem ranks below an actual one.
perOption.c: Coarse crackles with a weak cough mean secretions are retained now; this threatens oxygenation and leads to atelectasis and pneumonia.
perOption.d: Psychosocial needs follow physiological ones.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply ABC and Maslow priorities to nursing problems.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings on four clients who had procedures today. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?

options.text: A client 3 hours after a bronchoscopy whose gag reflex has returned and who is coughing up blood-tinged sputum
A client 4 hours after a colonoscopy with polyp removal whose abdomen is firm with guarding; heart rate 110/min
A client 2 hours after removal of 3 L of ascitic fluid whose blood pressure is 110/68, from 116/72 before the procedure
A client 1 hour after a thoracentesis with a small amount of serous drainage on the puncture-site dressing

rationale.correct: Compare each finding with what the procedure normally causes. Abdominal rigidity or guarding with tachycardia after any bowel procedure suggests perforation.

perOption.a: A small amount of blood-tinged sputum is expected after a bronchoscopy, especially after a biopsy.
perOption.b: A firm, guarded abdomen with tachycardia after polypectomy suggests bowel perforation and peritonitis.
perOption.c: A small drop after paracentesis needs monitoring but is within an expected range.
perOption.d: Minor drainage at the puncture site is expected.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish expected findings from complications after procedures.

questions.stem: The nurse has just received report on five clients and has one assistive personnel to help. Place the clients in the order the nurse should see them, from first to last.

items.text: A client with diabetes who is sweaty and shaky with a glucose of 58 mg/dL but alert and able to swallow
A client 3 hours after a thyroidectomy who has new noisy breathing on inspiration and an SpO2 of 91%
A client 2 hours after a hysterectomy with a heart rate of 124/min, blood pressure 88/50 and a saturated dressing
A client with stable heart failure who needs discharge teaching before going home this afternoon
A client 1 day after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy rating shoulder pain 7 out of 10 who is due for oral oxycodone

rationale.correct: Order by airway, then breathing and circulation, then other urgent physiological needs that are quick to fix, then expected discomfort, then teaching.

perOption.a: Stridor after neck surgery is an airway emergency and comes first.
perOption.b: Hemorrhage with signs of shock is the circulation threat; it follows only the airway.
perOption.c: Symptomatic hypoglycemia needs treatment within minutes, but the client can take oral glucose, which the nurse can give quickly.
perOption.d: Referred shoulder pain from the gas used in laparoscopy is expected; it needs treatment but is not dangerous.
perOption.e: Teaching a stable client is important but can wait until urgent needs are met.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Order several clients by priority.

questions.stem: The RN is planning care for a medical-surgical unit with assistive personnel (AP). Which tasks can the RN delegate to the AP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Measuring and recording intake and output for a client with heart failure
Checking placement of a nasogastric tube before an intermittent tube feeding
Walking a client 2 days after surgery who walked yesterday without problems
Feeding a client with a new stroke at the first meal after a swallowing evaluation
Obtaining a fingerstick glucose on a stable client before lunch
Taking the first vital signs of a client who arrived from surgery 10 minutes ago

rationale.correct: Delegate routine tasks with predictable outcomes for stable clients. Assessment, judgments such as tube placement, and care with a high or unpredictable risk stay with licensed nurses.

perOption.a: Measuring and recording I&O is a routine task with a predictable outcome; the RN interprets the totals.
perOption.b: Verifying tube placement needs assessment and judgment, so it stays with a licensed nurse.
perOption.c: Ambulating a stable client who has already walked safely is within the AP role.
perOption.d: The first meal after a dysphagia evaluation carries a high aspiration risk and needs a licensed nurse to watch the swallow.
perOption.e: Point-of-care glucose testing on a stable client is a routine, delegable task once the AP is trained; the RN acts on the result.
perOption.f: The first post-operative check is part of the RN's initial assessment of a client who may be unstable.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose tasks that can be delegated to assistive personnel.

questions.stem: The RN is making assignments for the shift with an LPN and assistive personnel. For each task, choose the staff member the RN should assign it to: the person with the most limited scope who can do the task safely.

rows.text: First assessment of a client transferred from intensive care 1 hour ago
Giving scheduled oral digoxin to a stable client whose apical pulse is 78/min
Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter in a stable client
Applying sequential compression devices to a client 1 day after surgery
Hanging a unit of packed red blood cells
Reinforcing low-sodium diet teaching that the RN started yesterday

rationale.correct: RNs keep initial assessment, unstable clients, blood products and the plan of care. LPNs give medications and do procedures for stable clients and reinforce teaching. APs do routine tasks with predictable outcomes.

perOption.r1:c1: A transfer from intensive care needs an RN's initial assessment.
perOption.r1:c2: LPNs collect data but cannot do the initial assessment of a client whose condition may change.
perOption.r2:c1: The RN could, but the task is within LPN scope.
perOption.r2:c2: Giving oral medications and checking the apical pulse for a stable client is within LPN scope.
perOption.r2:c3: APs do not give medications in acute care.
perOption.r3:c1: The RN could, but a sterile procedure for a stable client is within LPN scope.
perOption.r3:c2: Catheter insertion in a stable client is an LPN skill.
perOption.r3:c3: Catheter insertion is a sterile, invasive procedure outside the AP role in most facilities.
perOption.r4:c1: This does not need RN skills.
perOption.r4:c2: This does not need LPN skills.
perOption.r4:c3: Applying compression devices to a stable client is a routine AP task.
perOption.r5:c1: Starting a transfusion and watching the first 15 minutes for a reaction needs RN assessment.
perOption.r5:c2: In most states LPNs may not start blood products.
perOption.r6:c1: The RN could, but reinforcing teaching is within LPN scope.
perOption.r6:c2: LPNs reinforce teaching an RN has started.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match tasks to the scope of the RN, LPN and AP.

questions.stem: The RN is making assignments on a medical-surgical unit and has one LPN on the team. Which client is most appropriate to assign to the LPN?

options.text: A client returned from the post-anesthesia unit 1 hour ago after a bowel resection
A client on a heparin infusion whose aPTT result is due now with a rate change by protocol
A client with heart failure going home this afternoon who needs teaching about three new medications
A client with type 2 diabetes who needs correction-scale insulin and a foot-ulcer dressing change

rationale.correct: Assign the LPN stable clients with predictable outcomes and standard procedures. Keep new post-op clients, high-alert titrations and initial teaching with the RN.

perOption.a: A client in the first hours after surgery can change quickly and needs RN assessment.
perOption.b: Titrating a high-alert infusion by protocol needs RN judgment.
perOption.c: Discharge teaching about new medications is an RN responsibility.
perOption.d: This client is stable, and the care uses standard procedures within LPN scope.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assign clients appropriately to an LPN.

questions.stem: A nurse who usually works in pediatrics is floated to an adult medical-surgical unit for the shift. Which client should the charge nurse assign to this nurse?

options.text: A client 1 day after a thoracotomy with a chest tube to suction
A client with cellulitis of the leg receiving IV cefazolin every 8 hours
A client with new atrial fibrillation on a diltiazem infusion being titrated
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion adjusted hourly

rationale.correct: Give a float nurse stable clients whose care does not need the unit's specialist skills.

perOption.a: A new chest tube after chest surgery needs experience with adult surgical complications.
perOption.b: This stable client's care uses skills any RN has, so it suits a nurse from another unit.
perOption.c: Titrating a cardiac infusion for a new dysrhythmia needs adult cardiac experience.
perOption.d: Hourly insulin titration with electrolyte replacement is complex, unstable care.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assign appropriate clients to a float nurse.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that a client 1 day after a hip replacement has a blood pressure of 168/98 mm Hg. Two hours ago it was 132/80 mm Hg. The client has a PRN prescription for IV hydralazine if the systolic pressure is above 160 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the AP to recheck the blood pressure with a larger cuff in 15 minutes
Give the PRN hydralazine, because the reading meets the prescribed limit
Go to the client, recheck the pressure and look for pain or a full bladder
Document the reading and ask the AP to report it again at the next check

rationale.correct: The RN stays accountable for data the AP collects. An unexpected value needs the nurse's own reassessment, including common reversible causes, before treatment.

perOption.a: A wrong cuff size is possible, but asking the AP to recheck later delays the nurse's own assessment of a large change.
perOption.b: The order applies to a confirmed reading; the nurse must verify the value and look for a cause first.
perOption.c: The nurse verifies AP-collected data that shows a large change, and pain or urinary retention commonly raise blood pressure after surgery.
perOption.d: A significant change must be acted on now, not at the next routine check.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Follow up on abnormal data reported by assistive personnel.

questions.stem: The nurse is delegating vital sign checks to assistive personnel for a client who returned from a bowel resection 2 hours ago. Which instruction to the AP is best?

options.text: "Take his vital signs every 30 minutes, and let me know if anything changes."
"Take his vital signs every hour and chart them, and I will review the chart each hour."
"Take his vital signs every hour; if the pressure is low, lay him flat and recheck."
"Every hour, take his vitals; tell me at once if systolic is under 100 or pulse over 110."

rationale.correct: Good delegation states what to do, how often, and exactly which findings to report, and when.

perOption.a: The AP may not know what counts as a significant change for this client.
perOption.b: This gives no criteria for reporting, so a dangerous value could sit in the chart until the nurse looks.
perOption.c: This asks the AP to judge and intervene, which needs nursing assessment.
perOption.d: A clear frequency and specific values to report meet the right-communication part of delegation.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give clear, specific instructions when delegating.

questions.stem: The nurse asks an assistive personnel to insert a straight urinary catheter for a stable client, as the facility's policy allows for trained AP. The AP says, "I haven't been checked off on that yet." What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Show the AP the steps at the bedside first, then have the AP insert it while the nurse watches closely
Ask another AP who has been checked off to coach this AP through the procedure
Insert the catheter or give it to competent staff, and tell the manager about the training need
Reassign some of the AP's other clients so the AP has time to look the procedure up

rationale.correct: Under the right-person rule of delegation, the delegatee must be competent and validated. The nurse remains responsible for making sure the care is done.

perOption.a: Competency must be validated through the facility's process, not taught for the first time on a client who needs care now.
perOption.b: Another AP cannot supervise or validate competence.
perOption.c: Only a competent delegatee may do a task; the nurse makes sure the care happens and reports the training gap.
perOption.d: Reading about a procedure does not establish competence.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond when a delegatee lacks competence for a task.

questions.stem: The nurse is calling the surgeon at 0200 about a client 2 days after a bowel resection whose urine output has fallen. Place the nurse's statements in SBAR order, from first to last.

items.text: "I'm calling about Mr. Lee in room 12. His urine output has been 15 mL an hour for 3 hours."
"He is 2 days after a bowel resection, and his IV has been running at 75 mL an hour since surgery."
"Would you prescribe a fluid bolus and a basic metabolic panel, and see him within the hour?"
"His pressure is 96/60, pulse 108 and his mouth is dry. I think he is volume depleted."

rationale.correct: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) puts the reason for the call first and ends with a clear request, so nothing important is lost at night.

perOption.a: Situation: what is happening now.
perOption.b: Background: the relevant history and treatment.
perOption.c: Assessment: the nurse's findings and interpretation.
perOption.d: Recommendation: what the nurse thinks is needed.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Structure communication with a provider using SBAR.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving end-of-shift handoff on a client 1 day after a lobectomy. Which information is most important for the oncoming nurse?

options.text: The PCA morphine was stopped at 1600 and the first dose of oral oxycodone was given at 1630
The family wants an update from the surgeon at morning rounds tomorrow
The client walked in the hall twice and ate most of the dinner tray
SpO2 fell to 89% at 1500, oxygen was started at 2 L/min and a blood gas is pending

rationale.correct: Lead the handoff with changes in condition, new treatments and results still pending, because these need action on the next shift.

perOption.a: The pain plan change matters, and the oncoming nurse needs it, but the client is not unstable because of it.
perOption.b: This is a reasonable request to pass on but does not affect safety tonight.
perOption.c: Progress is useful context but needs no follow-up.
perOption.d: A change in condition with a new treatment and a pending result needs the oncoming nurse's follow-up first.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify priority information for a handoff report.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a left-sided stroke has a wet, gurgling voice after sips of water and coughs during meals. The family asks whether the client should switch to thickened liquids. Which referral should the nurse request?

options.text: Registered dietitian
Occupational therapist
Speech-language pathologist
Respiratory therapist

rationale.correct: A wet voice and coughing with fluids suggest dysphagia and aspiration risk. The speech-language pathologist evaluates the swallow and sets the diet consistency.

perOption.a: The dietitian plans nutrition and can adjust textures once a swallowing plan exists, but does not evaluate the swallow.
perOption.b: OT helps with self-feeding and adaptive utensils, not the swallow itself.
perOption.c: The SLP evaluates swallowing and decides on liquid consistency and safe-swallow techniques.
perOption.d: RT manages airway clearance and breathing treatments, not dysphagia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Refer a client with dysphagia to the right discipline.

questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis has trouble buttoning clothes, opening jars and holding a fork because of hand deformities. Which team member is best suited to help with these problems?

options.text: Physical therapist
Occupational therapist
Home health aide
Social worker

rationale.correct: Occupational therapy focuses on activities of daily living, fine motor tasks and adaptive equipment.

perOption.a: PT works on walking, strength and range of motion of large joints.
perOption.b: OT helps clients do daily activities with adaptive equipment such as button hooks and built-up utensils.
perOption.c: An aide can help with care but does not provide adaptive training or equipment.
perOption.d: Social workers help with resources, finances and coping.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Refer a client to occupational therapy for ADL limitations.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing data for clients on a medical unit. Which findings meet common criteria for calling the rapid response team? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client who was alert 1 hour ago is now confused and pulling at the IV
SpO2 of 89% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula with respirations of 28/min
Heart rate of 138/min that started 20 minutes ago
Urine output of 40 mL total over the last 4 hours
Systolic pressure of 96 mm Hg in a client whose baseline is 98 mm Hg
Temperature of 38.3 °C (100.9 °F) with a heart rate of 88/min

rationale.correct: Call the rapid response team for acute changes in mental status, breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygenation or urine output, before an arrest happens. Compare values with the client's baseline.

perOption.a: An acute change in mental status is an early warning sign of deterioration.
perOption.b: Hypoxemia despite oxygen with tachypnea meets rapid response criteria.
perOption.c: A sustained heart rate above 130/min is a common trigger.
perOption.d: Output below about 50 mL over 4 hours is a common trigger because it suggests poor perfusion.
perOption.e: This low-normal value matches the client's baseline.
perOption.f: A fever with a normal heart rate needs follow-up but does not meet rapid response criteria on its own.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize criteria for calling a rapid response team.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews morning laboratory results for six clients. Highlight the results that require the nurse's immediate follow-up.

cells: Client with chronic kidney disease, no ECG changes
Client taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation
Client admitted with an upper GI bleed
Hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, down from 9.6 g/dL last evening
Client 1 day after a hip replacement
Client with type 1 diabetes before breakfast

rationale.correct: Look at the trend and the client, not only the number: a falling hemoglobin, a supratherapeutic INR and hypoglycemia need action now; a mildly abnormal value expected for the condition can wait.

perOption.r1: A mildly raised potassium is common in chronic kidney disease and is not critical without ECG changes.
perOption.r2: An INR well above the 2 to 3 target raises bleeding risk; the provider needs to know before the next dose.
perOption.r3: A fall of nearly 2 g/dL overnight shows active bleeding, even though the value is above 7.
perOption.r4: A mild rise in white cells is common after surgery.
perOption.r5: A glucose below 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and needs treatment now, even without symptoms.
perOption.r6: This sodium is within the normal range.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify laboratory results that need immediate action.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four phone messages from clients seen this week. Which call should the nurse return first?

options.text: A client started on lisinopril 3 days ago who reports a dry, tickling cough
A client taking oxycodone after surgery who has not had a bowel movement in 3 days
A client discharged after a TURP yesterday who is passing clots and cannot urinate
A client 1 week after a knee arthroscopy with mild swelling around the knee and pain of 3

rationale.correct: Return first the call that describes a possible complication needing same-day care: urinary retention with active bleeding after prostate surgery.

perOption.a: A dry cough is a common ACE-inhibitor effect that needs a medication review but is not urgent; facial or tongue swelling would be.
perOption.b: Opioid constipation needs teaching and a laxative but is not urgent.
perOption.c: Clots with inability to void suggest obstruction and bleeding; bladder distention worsens bleeding and needs urgent care.
perOption.d: Mild swelling and pain around the joint are expected at this point.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize telephone follow-up calls.

questions.stem: The RN is working with an LPN on a medical-surgical unit. Which 2 tasks can the RN assign to the LPN?

options.text: Reinforcing the foot-care teaching the RN gave a client with diabetes
Giving a scheduled intramuscular injection to a stable client
Teaching a client newly prescribed insulin how to draw up a dose
Assessing a client who has just returned to the unit from surgery
Evaluating how a client is responding to a new antihypertensive

rationale.correct: LPNs give medications to stable clients and reinforce teaching. Initial assessment, initial teaching and evaluation stay with the RN.

perOption.a: Reinforcing teaching the RN has done is within LPN scope.
perOption.b: Giving IM medications to stable clients is within LPN scope.
perOption.c: Initial teaching is an RN responsibility.
perOption.d: The first post-op assessment of a client who may be unstable belongs to the RN.
perOption.e: Evaluating the outcome of care is an RN responsibility.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose tasks within the LPN's scope.

questions.stem: The RN is giving assignments to assistive personnel at the start of the shift. Which instruction from the RN is inappropriate?

options.text: "Please help Mr. Ruiz shower, and tell me if he gets short of breath."
"Please record how much Ms. Patel drinks and urinates during your shift."
"Please turn Mr. Ali every 2 hours and tell me about any reddened areas of skin."
"Please check Mrs. Chen's IV site and decide whether it needs restarting."

rationale.correct: APs can report what they observe, but deciding what an observation means is an assessment that stays with the nurse.

perOption.a: Hygiene care for a stable client with a clear reporting instruction is appropriate.
perOption.b: Measuring intake and output is an appropriate AP task.
perOption.c: Repositioning and reporting what is seen are appropriate AP tasks.
perOption.d: Deciding whether an IV must be restarted is an assessment and judgment the AP cannot make.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Avoid delegating assessment to assistive personnel.

questions.stem: One hour after an open cholecystectomy, a client rates incisional pain 8 out of 10, is nauseated and anxious, and has respirations of 22/min with fine crackles at both bases. The SpO2 is 88% on room air. The client has PRN prescriptions for IV morphine, IV ondansetron and oxygen. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Coach the client to use the incentive spirometer 10 times
Give the prescribed IV morphine for the pain
Raise the head of the bed and start the prescribed oxygen
Give the prescribed IV ondansetron for the nausea

rationale.correct: Treat the oxygenation problem first; anxiety and restlessness may themselves be signs of hypoxemia. Pain control and lung expansion follow.

perOption.a: Deep breathing helps the crackles, but the client is hypoxemic now and cannot breathe deeply with this pain; it comes after oxygen.
perOption.b: Pain relief will help the client breathe deeply, but an opioid can depress breathing further in a client who is already hypoxemic.
perOption.c: Hypoxemia is the most immediate threat, and positioning with oxygen improves it within minutes.
perOption.d: Nausea matters, but it is not the most dangerous problem.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize oxygenation among several post-op problems.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing three clients. For each client, select the finding that requires immediate follow-up.

groups.label: Client with COPD on 2 L/min of oxygen

options.text: SpO2 of 90%
New drowsiness with a morning headache
Increased anterior-posterior chest diameter

groups.label: Client 1 day after a total knee replacement

options.text: 120 mL in the wound drain over 8 hours
Calf 3 cm larger than the other leg and tender
Pain of 4 out of 10 after oral medication
Red, itchy flushing of the face and neck during the infusion
Trough level within the therapeutic range
Creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, unchanged from admission

rationale.correct: For each client, find the unexpected finding that signals a complication, and check abnormal-looking values against what is expected for that condition.

perOption.a: This is within the usual COPD target of 88% to 92%.
perOption.b: Drowsiness and headache suggest carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia).
perOption.c: A barrel chest is an expected long-term finding.
perOption.d: Drainage of this amount is expected in the first day.
perOption.e: One-sided calf swelling and tenderness suggest deep vein thrombosis.
perOption.g: This infusion reaction usually means the rate is too fast; stop or slow the infusion and notify the provider.
perOption.h: A therapeutic trough shows correct dosing.
perOption.i: Stable kidney function is reassuring with a nephrotoxic drug.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify findings that need follow-up across several clients.

questions.stem: At the start of a day shift on a medical unit, the nurse has four tasks. Which task should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give a scheduled third-day dose of IV cefazolin that is now 30 minutes late
Check the glucose of a client whose rapid-acting insulin is due when the tray arrives
Call the pharmacy about a missing dose of levothyroxine
See a 70-year-old woman with diabetes who told the AP she has jaw pain and nausea

rationale.correct: A possible acute coronary syndrome comes before scheduled tasks, and its atypical signs (jaw pain, nausea, fatigue) are common in women, older adults and people with diabetes.

perOption.a: A slightly late scheduled antibiotic matters, but it is not as time-critical as possible ischemia.
perOption.b: This is time-sensitive, but the meal has not arrived and it can follow the assessment.
perOption.c: Missing levothyroxine for a short time is not dangerous; another team member can make the call.
perOption.d: Jaw pain with nausea can be acute coronary syndrome, which women and people with diabetes often have without chest pain.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
